claim_text: **Yes, AI coding assistants can reduce software-development task completion time.
The effect is not universal.** Randomized studies show substantial time savings in some settings and a measurable slowdown in another.

| **Peng et al. (2023):** 95 professional programmers randomized to use GitHub Copilot or work without it on a JavaScript HTTP-server task. | Among participants who finished, average completion time was **71 versus 161 minutes: a 55.8% reduction** (95% confidence interval: 21–89%).
Completion required passing automated tests. [](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.06590) | One standardized task.
The preferred adjusted estimate was approximately **21% less time**, but its confidence interval included no effect (*p*=0.086).
The unadjusted comparison was statistically significant. [](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.12944) | A bounded experimental task using internal Google tools, limiting generalization. |.
| **Becker et al., METR (2025):** 16 experienced open-source developers completed 246 real tasks in repositories they knew well.
Tasks were randomized to allow or prohibit AI. | AI access **increased completion time by 19%**.

Developers primarily used Cursor with Claude 3.5/3.7 Sonnet. [](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.09089) [](https://metr.org/blog/2026-02-24-uplift-update/) | A small, specialized developer sample and a particular generation of tools. |.
In February 2026, METR reported follow-up estimates suggesting **18% less time for returning developers and 4% less for newly recruited developers**, but both confidence intervals included no effect.
Evidence does not establish a universal reduction in development time or total project delivery time**.
METR (2026). [*We are Changing our Developer Productivity Experiment Design.*](https://metr.org/blog/2026-02-24-uplift-update/).
**AI coding assistants can improve code quality on specific tasks.

The evidence does not establish a consistent overall improvement.** Controlled studies report better functional correctness and readability in some settings, conflicting security outcomes, and no clear downstream maintainability benefit.

These results support a benefit for the tested task, but the vendor-conducted experiment measured one exercise and reviewer judgments, rather than production defects or actual maintenance costs. [](https://github.blog/news-insights/research/does-github-copilot-improve-code-quality-heres-what-the-data-says/).
**Security: conflicting evidence.** Perry and colleagues found that participants using a Codex-based assistant produced less secure solutions to security-related programming tasks.
**Security: conflicting evidence.** Perry and colleagues were more likely to believe their code was secure.

Conversely, Sandoval and colleagues’ study of 58 student programmers implementing a linked-list application in C found a comparatively small security impact: the assisted group’s critical-bug rate was no more than 10% above the control group’s.
Both evaluated early-generation assistants, limiting extrapolation to current tools. [](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.03622) [](https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity23/presentation/sandoval).

**Maintainability: no demonstrated improvement in a direct experiment.** A preregistered, two-phase study involving 151 participants, 95% professional developers, tested whether other developers could more easily extend AI-assisted code.
A null result is not proof of equivalence or long-term safety. [](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10664-026-10889-1).
These are quality proxies, not confirmed production failures.
Quality should be judged separately across those outcomes, rather than inferred from faster coding or greater output. [1–5].
Perry, N., et al. (2023). [*Do Users Write More Insecure Code with AI Assistants?*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.03622) ACM CCS.
